book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Dracula's century-long grip on popular culture says more about us than about the Count, asking why we willingly seek out an evening of nightmares in Stoker's novel and its movie spin-offs when, as Van Helsing's failures show, Dracula just cannot be killed. It frames the volume's guiding questions: is Dracula truly evil, is his taste for human blood really worse than our meat-eating, and what does our fascination with this outdated, oddly accented aristocrat expose hidden in our own subconscious?

Mahon argues that vampiric immortality is a curse not because it brings decrepitude (against Swift's Struldbruggs model, since Dracula and his brides keep eternal youth) but because intelligent vampires know endless boredom awaits: following Bernard Williams and Shelly Kagan, boredom replaces death as the inevitable evil, giving vampires a Heideggerian 'being-toward-undeath' and 'being-toward-endless-pain'. Dracula's risky move from castle, brides, and slaves in Transylvania to London is read as the boredom escape it is, and since vampires still resist destruction, Mahon weighs the tedium curse against the alternative curse of compelled psychopathic bloodlust, concluding that staking Dracula is involuntary euthanasia - a mercy killing.

Pramik maps Kierkegaard's three stages from Either/Or and Stages on Life's Way onto the novel: Dracula lives the aesthetic stage of pleasure and possessive power (imprisoning Harker in the castle, refusing to let the brides feed on him), Harker the anxious ethical stage of moral rules and guilt, and Van Helsing the religious stage of faith 'by virtue of the absurd' - trusting God to do the impossible through crucifixes, garlic, and the beheading of Lucy. Against Seward's doubting questions about these absurd tactics, she argues that Van Helsing's renewed, tested faith proves itself and makes him the book's real hero, since neither pleasure nor ethics alone defeats Dracula or gives life meaning.

Willis and Strunk read the scene where Dracula forces Mina to drink blood from his bare chest through Plotinus's Enneads: the mutual blood exchange is a dark unicity, a perverted oneness joining life and death, through which the soulless, blood-dependent Count tries to steal Mina's agency, Intellect, and her link to the world soul because he cannot be self-sufficient or create his own meaning. Their interconnected minds are also his undoing - Mina's hypnotic bond tracks Dracula to his coffin, and his destruction at Van Helsing's hands frees her - so the chapter concludes that this perversion of Plotinian oneness exposes our fear that the veil between the living and the dead is dangerously thin.

Jordan asks what makes Dracula obey his rules (no entry without an invitation, native soil, garlic, the crucifix) when he obeys no morality: self-imposed Kantian moral rules and a vampire-cabal enforcing Hohfeldian duties both fail because the Count's self-interest is too strong, so the rules must be natural law set by God or nature. He then uses Wesley Hohfeld's jural relations (duty, claim, liberty, power, immunity, liability, disability) to analyze Dracula's rule over his brides, servants, and victims - Lucy's lost consent shifting power and letting the Count through her door - concluding that only this legal-relations analysis plus natural law explains both Dracula's restraints and his apparent violations of physics like defying gravity and commanding the weather.

Arp starts from Dracula's inability to love or find satisfaction and his awareness of it, then deploys Sidgwick's hedonistic paradox: pursuing pleasure for its own sake yields pain whether or not the pleasure is found, through mistaking pain for pleasure (Lestat on the dead twins), boredom, or emptiness. Mill's distinction between lower bodily and higher mental pleasures explains how vampires can enjoy the bodily pleasure of blood yet lament lacking joy and love, while substance versus property dualism (Plato as the substance dualist) frames whether the Count's soul survives when his body crumbles to dust. Aristotle's Book X pleasures of completed states and the 'virtuous vampires' from Barnabas Collins to St. Germain show the only escape from the dilemma: pursue activities for their own sake and higher mental pleasures rather than bodily pleasure alone.

Littmann turns vampirism into a thought experiment against meat-eating, using Jonathan's delight in the Hotel Royale chicken as the double standard: every justification for the Count preying on humans - might makes right, his superior intelligence and cunning, an arbitrary threshold of cleverness, or the human soul and its afterlife - would equally license beings superior to us (supernaturally strong, centuries-cunning Dracula himself) to prey on humans. Following Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', he argues the real wrong of vampirism is the net suffering it creates, and this utilitarian standard equally condemns factory farming, pushing us toward humanely raised meat or vegetarianism.

Altmann stages a moral (not legal) trial of Dracula with three expert witnesses: Kant testifies that Dracula universalizes murder only for himself while fleeing Harker's kukri, and that he reduced Harker to a mere meal, violating the categorical imperative and deserving execution; Mill weighs consequences, tallying the misery done to Lucy, her mother, and the Bloofer Lady's child victims, and argues the greatest happiness lies in imprisoning the Count for medical study instead; Aristotle argues the child-brained vampire lacks the reason and self-control needed for eudaimonia and so merits imprisonment rather than death. The chapter hands the verdict to the reader, showing guilt is agreed but punishment diverges across the three frameworks.

Bowman argues through Arendt that Dracula is not inherently evil but thoughtless: like Eichmann he cannot think from another's standpoint, treats people as cogs and means (Harker as captive, humans as prey), uses violence as a constructive tool, and protects himself with rhetorical safeguards like 'Enter freely' so he need never face his own cruelty. Measured against the Crew of Light's thoughtfulness - Harker's memos and recipes for Mina, Mina's care for Lucy, the suitors' gentlemanly bonds - the Count's evil is banal, lazy, 'Evil Lite'; but because Dracula stands outside humanity and knows humans only as livestock, Bowman concludes that Eichmann is banal yet truly evil, while Dracula, though careless, can never be evil.

Altmann asks whether Dracula is blameworthy for his killings: John Martin Fischer's guidance control, Kant's reason-centered morality, and Hume's 'yay/boo' approval-and-disapproval theory (the heroes' anguish over Mina) all seem to condemn him, since the Count coolly plans feedings and uses his intellect for evil. But Nagel-style luck undermines all three accounts, because Dracula never consented to his transformation, lacks the conscience needed to even recognize right and wrong, and, like the holy-wafer-branded Mina, is fixed by God's rejection with no hope of redemption - so the chapter concludes Dracula is evil yet a victim of circumstance deserving no full blame.

Michaud reads the novel through Nietzsche: the Crew of Light are resentful sheep banding together to kill a lion, damning Dracula not for wrongdoing but for his will-to-power, his hunting, and his reproduction - things humans do daily to animals - while the tale's enduring popularity over Nietzsche's heresy proves the death of God never happened, since we still use religion to console ourselves about dying. Following Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, he argues Dracula stories are humanity's immortality project: we must narrate the destruction of physical immortality to persuade ourselves it is a curse ('it would suck to be immortal') and that heroic, spiritual salvation in heaven is the better eternity.

McKinney argues Van Helsing should have studied Dracula's brain instead of staking him, because the Count is a philosophy-of-mind thought experiment: a mind that persists unchanged across bat, wolf, mist, and human bodies refutes mind-brain identity theory and fits functionalism (the mind as one song playable in many formats), while his telepathic bond with Mina and shapeshifting probe Cartesian dualism's mind-body interaction problem. Nagel's bats show that only Dracula could tell us what it is like to echo-locate or wolf-sense; yet since nothing like his unconstrained mind exists in our world, the novel finally maps what minds are not - evidence against the immaterial mind.

McCrossin uses Locke's memory theory of personal identity - consciousness extending to past and future actions, with 'all the right and justice of reward and punishment' founded in it - to ask whether Dracula is a monster but still a person, illustrated by an imagined Quincey-Seward body swap where only the mind that remembers the deed deserves blame. Mina, midway between human and vampire and fearing for her own future personhood, supplies the empathy and pity ('that poor soul') that turn the crew's campaign into one of mercy - they weep and grant the Count a peaceful death - adding a sentimental middle ground that Locke's claim that morality is demonstrable like mathematics cannot account for.

Wolfe asks what makes Stoker's mustachioed Count, Lugosi's, Dell Comics' science-hero Dracula, The Electric Company's malt-drinker, Blade's Drake, and Hotel Transylvania's overprotective dad all 'Dracula'. Plato's theory of Forms promises a shared ideal essence, but comparing particulars (origins from Vlad Tepes to Judas Iscariot, blood-drinking vs vanilla malts) finds no common thread, his 'Allegory of Dracula's Dungeon' recasts the cave to suggest Dracula may be only a shadow of some other Form like 'the undead', and the Republic's condemnation of art as imitation of imitation implies a fictional character may have no Form at all. Wolfe's own answer: the ideal Dracula is an outsider, an aristocrat, and a feeder on others, with everything else up for grabs.

holes.name: Wesley Hohfeld
holes.what: Early twentieth-century American legal philosopher who analyzed legal and rule-governed relationships into eight jural elements: duty, claim, liberty, power, liability, immunity, and disability.
holes.why: Chapter 12's conclusion that Dracula's house-invitation rule and his dominance over brides, servants, and victims are best explained rests on Hohfeldian jural relations combined with natural law.

holes.name: John Martin Fischer
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of free will who argues that 'guidance control' - acting from one's own reasons and desires even if only one path is available - is sufficient for moral responsibility.
holes.why: Chapter 18's case for holding Dracula blameworthy despite his cursed, conscienceless nature is built directly on Fischer's guidance-control account, which the chapter then argues fails for Dracula.

holes.name: Ernest Becker
holes.what: Cultural anthropologist and author of The Denial of Death (1973), which holds that human civilization is an 'immortality project' - a vast distraction and heroism system for evading the terror of our own deaths.
holes.why: Chapter 19's central reading of Dracula - as a story in which weak humans kill physical immortality to deny mortality and secure spiritual immortality - is explicitly grounded in Becker's death-denial theory.

holes.name: Functionalism (multiple realizability of mind)
holes.what: The view that a mind is whatever performs the mental function, regardless of its physical substrate - so one and the same mind can be realized in wildly different bodies (against mind-brain identity theory).
holes.why: Chapter 21's core argument is that Dracula's mind remaining his own across bat, wolf, mist, and human bodies refutes brain-identity theory and is best captured by the functionalist 'same song, many formats' picture, which no existing taxonomy slug names.
